questions.q: What is the NumPy broadcasting rule for comparing two array shapes?
options: Shapes must always be identical, or an error is raised
Compare dimensions from the trailing (rightmost) side; they're compatible if equal or if one of them is 1
The smaller array is always padded with zeros to match the larger one
Broadcasting only works on 1-dimensional arrays
questions.explain: NumPy compares shapes starting from the trailing dimension; two dimensions are compatible if they're equal or if one of them is 1, which then stretches to match without copying data.

questions.q: When a shape-(5,) array is broadcast against a shape-(250, 5) array in `returns - col_mean`, what actually happens in memory?
options: col_mean is duplicated 250 times into a new (250, 5) array before subtracting
NumPy reuses the single (5,) row for each of the 250 rows without physically duplicating it
The operation fails because the shapes don't match
returns is reshaped to (5, 250) first
questions.explain: Broadcasting is cheap precisely because NumPy reuses the smaller array's data across the larger shape rather than physically copying it into a full-size array.

questions.q: Why is `array.T` (transpose) essentially instant even on very large arrays?
options: NumPy only transposes the first row for performance
Transpose is computed lazily and never actually happens
It returns a view with swapped strides over the same underlying memory, rather than copying any data
Transpose only works on arrays smaller than 1000 elements
questions.explain: Transposing swaps the array's stride metadata (how many bytes to skip per axis) without moving any underlying data, which is why it's effectively free regardless of array size.

questions.q: A slice `sl = arr[2:5]` is mutated with `sl[0] = 999`. What happens to `arr[2]`, and why?
options: arr[2] is unchanged, because slicing always copies
arr[2] becomes 999, because a basic slice returns a view that shares memory with arr
This raises an error because views are read-only
arr[2] becomes 999 only if .copy() was called first
questions.explain: Basic slicing returns a view sharing the same memory buffer as the original array, so mutating the view also mutates the original. Fancy indexing, by contrast, returns a copy.

questions.q: What does `np.shares_memory(a, b)` tell you, and how does fancy indexing (e.g. `arr[[2, 3, 4]]`) differ from basic slicing with respect to it?
options: It checks if a and b have the same dtype; fancy indexing always matches
It checks if two arrays overlap in the same underlying memory buffer; fancy indexing returns a copy (shares_memory is False), while basic slicing returns a view (shares_memory is True)
It checks if two arrays have the same shape; both indexing styles always return True
It is only meaningful for arrays created with np.zeros
questions.explain: np.shares_memory reports whether two arrays' data overlaps. Basic slices are views (shares memory), while fancy indexing with a list or boolean mask always produces an independent copy.
